content_html:
NASA's next major astrophysics observatory is being prepared for a mission built around a simple advantage: seeing more sky at once. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, named for NASA's first chief astronomer and a key architect of the Hubble program, is moving through final launch preparations ahead of a SpaceX Falcon Heavy flight from Kennedy Space Center.

Roman is not designed to replace Hubble or the James Webb Space Telescope. Instead, it will occupy a different observational niche, combining Hubble-class mirror size with an unusually broad field of view and infrared sensitivity. The result will be a survey telescope capable of connecting individual galaxies, exploding stars, and exoplanet systems to the larger structure of the universe.

Wide Field Vision | How Roman Differs From Hubble

Roman's primary mirror is 2.4 meters across, the same diameter as Hubble's. The key difference is what happens after light reaches the mirror. Roman's wide-field optics feed a camera with approximately 300 megapixels, allowing the observatory to capture a much larger patch of sky in one exposure.

Hubble behaves like a powerful telephoto lens. It produces detailed images of relatively narrow targets, which is ideal for resolving individual galaxies, stellar nurseries, and distant planetary systems. Roman behaves more like a high-resolution panoramic camera. Its surveys will cover broad regions repeatedly, creating statistical samples large enough to measure how galaxies and cosmic structures change across time.

NASA's Roman mission briefing describes an observatory intended to survey billions of galaxies, thousands of Type Ia supernovae, and millions of stars in the dense central regions of the Milky Way.

Wide Field Instrument | Mapping Dark Energy

The Wide Field Instrument, or WFI, is Roman's primary scientific camera. Its infrared detectors will record light from galaxies that have traveled across the expanding universe, giving astronomers a way to measure how matter is distributed across enormous volumes of space.

One of Roman's central goals is to determine how the expansion of the universe has changed over time. Dark energy is the name given to the phenomenon associated with the universe's accelerating expansion, but its physical nature remains unknown. Roman will approach the question through several independent measurements, including weak gravitational lensing, galaxy clustering, and the distances to Type Ia supernovae.

Weak lensing measures the subtle distortion of background galaxy shapes caused by intervening matter. When repeated across billions of galaxies, those distortions reveal how dark matter has gathered into the cosmic web. Comparing that growth with the expansion history can test whether dark energy behaves like a cosmological constant or whether gravity itself requires a revised description on cosmic scales.

Microlensing | Finding Cold and Rogue Planets

Roman will also watch millions of stars toward the crowded inner Milky Way. When a foreground star or planet passes almost directly between a distant star and the telescope, its gravity bends and magnifies the background starlight. This temporary brightening is called gravitational microlensing.

Microlensing is especially useful for finding planets that are difficult to detect with the methods used by many current observatories. The event can reveal worlds on wide orbits, planets far from the heat of their host stars, and objects that have been ejected from planetary systems altogether. These free-floating or rogue planets may be invisible in ordinary reflected light, but their gravity can briefly announce their presence.

The survey will help answer whether the solar system's architecture is typical. A large population of cold planets would show that planetary systems commonly extend well beyond the orbits of their warm inner worlds. A substantial rogue population would also reveal how often gravitational encounters dismantle young planetary systems.

Coronagraph Instrument | Blocking Starlight to See Worlds

Roman carries a second instrument with a different purpose. The Coronagraph Instrument, or CGI, is a technology demonstration for high-contrast imaging. It uses masks to block the light of a bright host star and deformable mirrors that actively change shape to correct tiny optical errors.

Those mirrors can flex at nanometer scales. By adjusting the wavefront of incoming light, the instrument can suppress residual starlight that would otherwise overwhelm the much fainter glow of a planet. The demonstration is aimed primarily at Jupiter-like and ice giant worlds, not Earth analogs, but the techniques could inform future missions designed to search for and characterize smaller planets.
